The hon. gentleman stated also that this was a statistical Bill, an amalgamation of the census and statistics branches, that he was following the lines of the census law of the United States, the object of which he did not seem to understand. Then the minister speaks of the statistics gathered from the different provinces. What will be the result of the plan that he proposes to follow ? For instance, Ontario at the present time furnishes these agricultural statistics, so does Manitoba ; but as respects the other provinces, these statistics are to be procured at the federal expense. What will be the result ? The result will be that Ontario will say to this government, if you get this information at the expense of the Dominion for the other provinces while we have to pay for our own, we will drop our work, and you must pay for it the same as you do for the other provinces. All these things must be considered. The hon. gentleman brags about his census returns that he says he sent down to the printer so early that we will get it all in 1905, whereas the late government did not get their returns published till after 1897. He forgets to tell us the cost of the census of ten years ago, which was about half million dollars, and that of twenty years ago about $400,000, while his census up to the present time has cost about $1,200,000.
At six o'clock, committee took recess.
After Recess.
Committee resumed at eight o'clock.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I would like to inquire where we are. I understand that you reserved your decision on a point of order until to-morrow. Has it been decided that we shall proceed with the Bill before we get your decision as to the point of ol der ?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I understand that there was a kind of agreement entered into that the money clauses would not be taken up until the decision was rendered to-morrow.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: And that we shall go on with the other clauses ?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Go on with the others, if there is no objection.
Clause 1 is a mere title clause, and that is generally left until the end. I would, therefore, ask you, Mr. Chairman, to proceed with clause 2.

Before you proceed with clause 2, I would like to have a little more information on this Bill, because it seems to me we are not going to realize what the hon. minister told the House we might expect to realize ; that is, by adopting this method suggested now we would materially reduce the cost of taking the census at each decennial period, and that we would get the census much more correctly taken than at the present time. In answer to a question, I understood the hon. minister to say that one of the ways in which this would be accomplished would be the education of certain parties to do the work. In order to ascertain whether that might be accomplished or not I inquired whether it was intended to educate the enumerators. I understood the hon. minister to say that it was not, that there were only certain parties in the office who would be working at the census from year to year between the ten-year periods. So that the parties, above all others, who, in my opinion, would require education to get the work correctly and expeditiously done- the enumerators-would not be touched by any provision of this Bill. I did not understand the hon. minister to say that they would be in any way touched.
No ; I do not think so.

I am unable to agree with my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule). I would rather look upon a great deal of what he has brought forward as an endorsation of the objects of this Bill. He says, for instance, that there is certain information about labour, wages, &c., in the report of the Ontario Bureau of Mines, and we have also a labour bureau here which issues under the authority of the Dominion government-and I think that the publication of the ' Labour Gazette ' has been endorsed both by the House and the country-a compilation and statement of the condition of wages and labour in this country. Just as that report of the Labour Bureau is for the whole Dominion of Canada, while the report of the Bureau of Industries is for the province of Ontario alone, so the work that will be done under this Bill in regard to the several branches of industry referred to would be for the whole Dominion. The information to which the hon. gentleman referred is for the province of Ontario, but we want to get that information for the whole country. Then too, the report of the Bureau of Industry deals only with the agricultural and to a certain extent the mineral productions of the province, although the report of the Mr. SPROULE.
Bureau of Mines in Ontario gives certain information about the mining and mineral production in that province.
And the Geological Survey gives it for the whole Dominion.

The report of the Geological Survey does not deal very much with the actual production of minerals. The Geological Survey report is a report on scientific geological work more than on the production of minerals although it does deal with these figures to a certain extent. My hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) spoke of the returns of the Department of Inland Revenue. It is true that on certain lines the department gives a good deal of information in reference to articles connected with excise and taxation through excise, but it does not give the information about any other products, and the information which it does give us is with relation to the taxation more than with relation to the production. Incidentally it gives some statements' in regard to the products that enter into the production of liquor, cigarettes, &c., but still after all this is done in the Department of Inland Revenue with an eye to and in relation with the collection of revenue and not in connection with the products of industry.
So long as the information is given what difference does it make what the connection is ?

It gives that information and we would be able to make use of it for tabulated statements that might be drawn up in connection with the same subject, but not particularly with the production of revenue. My hon. friend will agree with me that the questions of tabulated statistics is practically interminable. It is possible to deal with a certain set of figures in many . different ways according to the object that the student for instance, may have in view. The figures collected by the Department of Inland Revenue are dealt with by that department for the purposes of the revenue, but that particular set of figures might not help the person wrho is studying the culture of barley for malting purposes. But still they would be identically the same figures in the original collection of information. My hon. friend says that certain labour statistics are collected by the provincial government of Ontario and certain other statistics of a different character altogether by the Inspectors of factories in the differont provinces, figures that are collected chiefly from a hygienic standpoint, having in view the safety of the operatives in factories, and yet these figures can be made use of in the reports of the Bureau of Labour here, and so collated as to show the condition of the workmen all over Canada. With the new system we will be able to furnish information on many subjects from a Dominion or national standpoint, using the information that is collected by the provincial auth-

orities ancl also that collected by various associations such as dairy associations which might collect various statistics in regard to the production of cheese and butter.
Is Ontario the only province that collects agricultural statistics ?
The province of Manitoba does a little, but not nearly so much as Ontario. I am not aware that any other province collects any.

I see here in the statistical year-book a table of live stock in Manitoba, giving the value each year. For 1897, JB98, 1899 and 1900 there is a complete statement of the value of stock in the province of Manitoba. The hon. gentleman's Bill would not encroach upon that ?
Not so far as Manitoba is concerned.
Are we to understand that that information is published only for Ontario and Manitoba ?

I know of no other. I do not think the hon. member will find it in regard to Quebec, the maritime provinces, British Columbia or the Territories, and the extent of agricultural information gathered in the province of Manitoba is not as great as that gathered in the province of Ontario. I have already referred to the point mentioned by my hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule), and I rather take most of what he has said to be an endorsation of a good deal of what is in this Bill.

That is not the interpretation that I intended to have put upon it. I said what I did because I have heard at different times almost the same line of reasoning with regard to other plans for collecting statistics. When we were asked to incur the expense of getting statistics for the Year-Book, we were told that it was for exactly the same purposes for which the hon. minister says we are now justified in incurring this expense. When it was proposed to have a monthly report from the Department of Trade and Commerce, we were told that it was in order to furnish statistics for the mercantile community. When the establishment of the Bureau of Labour was proposed, we were told that statistics were required from time to time to inform the wage earners of the country of the conditions of wages and labour, in different localities. The same argument has been put forward with regard to all these proposals, and the question that presented itself to my mind was whether we had not reached the limit of expenditure for the purpose of collecting and publishing statistics. The hon. minister says that figures can be arranged in a great variety of ways. I have no doubt that they can ; but is thaj: any justification for going on to devise other
ways of arranging them in order to spend | money ? I do not think it is.

If this Bill were going to repeat what has already (been done, my hon. friend's argument would be quite right ; but it is not. It is taking up work in other directions. The Trade and Com-| merce Reports, for instance, do not deal in any way with agriculture ; they deal only with trade and commerce, and with external commerce. They are compiled practically from the Trade and Navigation re-i turns, besides containing reports of our agents abroad. But they do not give any information about our home production. My hon. friend says this is exactly the argument that was put forward when the Year Book was established and when the Labour Bureau was proposed. I quite agree with my hon. friend. Parliament decided to establish the Year Book and the | Labour Bureau for specific purposes, and this Bill has a specific purpose in another direction. There is at present no provision for compiling the kind of information for the whole country that this Bill makes provision for. It is exactly on the same principle as the establishment of the Year Book and the Labour Bureau, and in that sense I venture to think that what my hon. friend has said is rather favourable to the principle of the Bill.

If I could see in what way it would benefit the country, I would be ready to support it, because I am in favour of correct statistics. The hon. minister does not propose to deal with all the products of the country at the same time, but he proposes to deal with one line in one year and with another line in another year. I do not see how that is going to be of any great benefit to the country at large. I could see how it might be of some use to ascertain all the products of the country over three or four years. The statistics must include everything, I think, to be of any great value. What I would like to understand is in what particular way this is going to benefit us ? What particular phase of it can we utilize, and thereby make more money ? We cannot follow the markets any more closely, we cannot diversify our pursuits any better, I take it.. If the information which we are getting from various sources to-day is as reliable as the proposed information will be, I do not see that it is going to be of much if any value. If I thought it was going to be an improvement, I would commend the establishment of a new system.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
I would like to ask the hon. minister, from what class of the community has the demand come for this legislation ? Has it come from the manufacturers, from the merchants, from the labouring classes, from the farmers ? The only class that has made any demand, so far as

X can see. is some gentlemen who want positions varying from $4,000 a year down, for the purpose of compiling some statistics. I have listened to the hon. minister very attentively, and he has failed to answer the question propounded by my hon. friend from South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox), as to what value these statistics, when gathered, will be to the great tax-paying class of the country, the farmers. Are they making any demand for this legislation, and in what way is it going to benefit them ? The hon. minister has signally failed to answer that question. I understood the hon. minister to say that he wanted to gather for the whole Dominion such information as that published in the province of Ontario by the Bureau of Industries.
How is my hon. friend going to get this information from the maritime provinces and the province of Quebec ? Does he think he will get it by sending out circulars ? Will the parties to whom these circulars are sent tell him how many cheese factories there are in the proviuce of Quebec. In my opinion, in no other way can the information be gathered except through the municipal assessors. If you have a jirovince in which there are no assessments taken, yon cannot get the information unless you send out a staff of your own. All I can see in this Bill is to furnish the minster with a pretext for employing a staff a few weeks before the election and sending them out to find how many grit and tory votes there are in the various constituencies. The hon. gentleman tells us that he will send out schedules to the manufacturers and will have a law passed compelling the manufacturers to answer the questions contained in these schedules. But why did lie not compel them to do this in the last census ? Many of them replied to his questions by saying: It is none of your business. He wanted them to divulge the secrets of their business, to tell the public how much goods of a certain kind they manufactured, how much money was invested in their business, what wages they paid per day; and lots of manufacturers refused to answer. But even if he had these schedules filled up, what benefit would that be to the manufacturers generally ? I can see no benefit to any class of our community from this expenditure of $20,000 the first year and double that amount the next year. You certainly cannot gather the information the hon. minister requires, except by employing a staff in each municipality to go from house to house and collect it. I am confident that our farmers will see no advantage to them in any such expenditure. That will not make their land produce an extra bushel of wheat or a cheese factory turn out an extra pound of cheese. The hon. minister should answer the question put him by the hon. member for Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) and tell us what benefit these statistics will be to the farmers, when gathered, and also Mr. TAYLOR.
from what class of the community comes any demand for this legislation.

We have had demands from all classes of the community and all parts of the country for the information we propose gathering.
Mr. TAYLOR, Will the hon. minister lay these demands on the table?
Surely the hon. gentleman does not want me to lay on the table the letters received by the department during the last ten years.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
We will take one year.
iMr. FISHER. Those demands come in all shapes and forms. Sometimes they are for information we are able to give and frequently for information not at our command, In the second place, the demand has not come from anybody seeking positions. There has been no demand for this particular measure, but I am introducing it in order to meet demands for information which we have not now the, power or the machinery to collect. This measure is a consolidation of three Acts now on the statutes, and very little additional machinery or power is required to carry out the object I have in view. The three Acts are for three different purposes, and are here consolidated into one, which will cover the whole ground and add some necessary powers to make them complete. I have the power to-day, under the General Statistics Act, to app'oint agents all over the country to collect information, and have only to ask parliament to **ote the money. Under the Census Act. I have the power every ten years to appoint enumerators and make a census.
Does the law give the hon .gentleman the right to take the census every six years in the Northwest?

Yes, and we are extending that power to the new provinces which are to be created. The intention is to take one census between each decennial census for those new provinces just as we are required to do by the Manitoba Act for Manitoba.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: But the five year census in Manitoba is simply to count the heads of the population for the purpose of ascertaining the amount that province is to receive per head.
Yes, but this measure goes further and extends to the new provinces to be created in the Northwest Territories.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
How is the hon. gentleman to get information from the other provinces which do not make a report as the Ontario Bureau of Industries does? When the office is fully equipped, how is he going to find out for instance, how many cheese factories tney have in New Brunswick, and

how many horses and cattle? How is he going to get it for the other provinces ?
These statistics for the province of Ontario to which my hon. friend (Mr. Taylor) refers are gathered largely by correspondence-by sending out forms-;-

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: No, no.

My hon. friend must not shake his head. These facts are not all taken from the assessors' returns by any means. Certain of them are, but not all. Some are secured by sending out circulars with questions and requests that the answers to these questions be given. There will be no difficulty in dealing with the subjects my hon. friend referred to in the case of such industries as the cheese and butter factories. That information, I know by experience-having tried to get it in individual instances and for particular localities-can be got perfectly well without an enumeration-it can be got in complete and accurate form. Similar information can be got in regard to other industries, just as it can folfactories or dairy products.
Does the hon. minister mean to say that the information for Ontario is got by sending out circulars ?
I understand that a good deal of that information is got in the way I have outlined.

I understood the minister to say that he would issue circulars promiscuously and so get that information. But that is not the way the information is secured for the Ontario Bureau of Industries. That information is obtained from municipal officers, who report to the bureau in response to its circulars. How else, for instance, would the hon. Minister of Agriculture obtain the assessment of a municipality ? Will he take it on a report of some farmer ? He must get such information, if he gets it at all from the municipal officers. * And so all along the line, as described by the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule).

If my hon. friend (Mr Ingram) will allow- me a moment ; He is right to a certain extent. The Bureau of Industries of Ontario publishes much information obtained from municipal officers. And the same kind of thing can be procured in the same way in the other provinces. In the province of Quebec there is a vast mass of municipal information available. I believe the same is true of some, if not all, the maritime provinces. This Act contemplates the collection of that information for these provinces in the same way that such information is collected in Ontario by the Bureau of Industries.

The hon. gentleman's (Mr. Fisher's) department already obtains information in that w-ay. He sends out circulars
from time to time asking concerning the success or failure of certain crops, for Instance, and, on the strength of the replies to these circulars, he prepares a bulletin. But, the hon. gentleman, as we understand him, says he is going to establish a Bureau tof Industries for the whole Dominion for $35,000. The hon. gentleman can no more do that than the sun can shine at mid-night. This is simply the thin end of the wedge, and, in the course of a year or so, instead of $35,000, we shall find an expenditure of $135,000. Up to this time the difficulty that this House has had, and that the country has had, is that the statistical year-book is laid on the table and is distributed among the people far too late. And, when you inquire into the cause of this delay, you find it in the fact that the government has starved the statistical department it already has. Sufficient force is not employed to expedite matters and push the year-book out in good time. Yet, the hon. minister is establishing a department that will conflict with the department he' already has. Why not spend the money in improving the existing department instead of establishing another ? Coming from Ontario, and as a representative of Ontario, I do not see why we in that province who pay for collecting and publishing our own statistics, slioul%be called upon to assist in publishing statistics for the rest of the Dominion.
I am sorry to have my hon. friend (Mr. Ingram) say in effect, that, so long as Ontario gets certain information the people of Ontario do not care whether the test of the Dominion gets it or not.
He did not say that.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Ingram) thought that the information secured for the province of Ontario was sufficient for that province. I believe that a large number of people in Ontario, as well as in the rest of the Dominion, want to get the same kind of information about the whole Dominion as is now collected for Ontario- information concerning our national industries and productions. For that reason, I think, it is necessary that this work should be done under the Dominion government. Each province now- collects a certain amount of information. Ontario collects a great deal, Manitoba a certain amount, Nova Scotia, Quebec and the rest, a certain amount. But I Ije information gathered varies, the method of making up the tables varies. When the Dominion office is established and collects that information from provincial and local sources, through assessment rolls, reports of municipal secretary-treasurers or in any other way, it will be able to collate that information in tables covering the whole Dominion.- I am quite sure that the people of Ontario are as anxious to have that information as are those of any other part of the Dominion.

I think the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) was scarcely fair to the Northwest Territories when he made the statement that agricultural statistics were collected only in the provinces of Ontario and Manitoba. For many years past the Department of Agriculture of the Northwest Territories has been collecting agricultural statistics, statistics which have proven accurate and which are of very great use not only to the farmers, but to all classes of the community. Especially have they been of use to us in making arrangements with the railway companies for carrying out our grain and in other matters of that character.

I think this committee should be very slow to pass a measure such as that now under consideration. I do not think that the minister has shown that the information he proposes to collect will be of any great service to the country. And, in any case, it is clear that he cannot collect that information at the expense he proposes. Statistics about Canada, to be useful, must be had promptly. There is no use in having the facts about last years crop presented to us next year. To be of service those figures must be had within a month or two ; and surely the*gninister does not seriously tell this committee that he can accomplish the collection and publication of statistics on this basis for any such sum as he has named. From the experience we had in connection with the last census, I think the committee may well hesitate long before handing over to the disposal of the minister any sum as he suggests for the carrying out of the purposes of this measure.
The census taken five years ago shows,
I think, the need of this committee going slow in placing a large sum of money at the disposal of the hou. gentleman. I have here the Auditor General's Report for the year after the census was taken. I turn over a few leaves, and when I see how lavish the hon. gentleman has been in the expenditure of public money, I am astonished, and yet I know what it all means. For instance, take page D-143, and what will he find there ?	' Commissioner for the
county of Inverness, N.S., Mr. J. G. McRae, $289.67 ; overpayment, $150.' What became of that $150? $150 was paid to that commissioner over what he ought to have got. I was running an election in my riding at that time, and I know what every one of these appointments of commissioners meant, I know why this large expenditure of money became necessary. I would like to know whether there was an attempt made to recover that $150 from this man. In opening this book I have struck this account at random, but there is enough here to show that this committee had better go slow in voting money to be spent by the hon. gentleman. Have we any reason to suppose that this information which he is
- going to collect will be forthcoming in time to be of any service to this country ? We have no assurance that it will be.

Section 2 is a very important one, and I wish to call the attention of the minister to a question involved in the consideration of this clause.
In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires, the word * minister ' means the Minister of Agriculture, and the word ' office ' means the census and statistics office.
Well, this is an important question, it is important for us to consider whether the minister who administers this Act is to be the Minister of Agriculture. To make plain what I am aiming at, I will refer to a line in the next section.
There shall be a permanent office under the Minister of Agriculture to be called the census and statistical office.
Now, I say that the time has come in Canada when, having regard to the large amount of money invested by the farmers in their operations, we shall have a whole, able-bodied Minister of Agriculture all to ourselves. The Minister of Agriculture himself has dealt with this question. It may be that he had in view some other Minister of Agriculture, and he thought that it might be proper to divide him. But in this case, on behalf of the farmers of this country, I protest in ail seriousness against dividing our Minister of Agriculture. Mark Twain, I think it is, tells us about the cannibals of some south sea islands who, as showing their appreciation of the missionary, came out of a ' restaurant ' smacking their lips, and saying he was a good, tender missionary, and they wished they had more of him. So far as I am concerned, having regard to the fact that the Minister of Agriculture has in the past been so distracted from the concerns of the great producing class in this country, I think we should take this matter seriously in hand now, and that we should consider, not whe-tiiere we shall enlarge the duties of the Minister of Agriculture, hut whether we shall not insist, so far as we can in a parliamentary way, on having some gentleman to represent the agricultural interest of this country who will be content with the glories attaching to that office, without desiring to grasp a large measure of glory from some other source. Now, to show the position we are in in regard to agriculture, I will quote from the mouth of a witness that cannot be disputed, I will take the liberty of reading from a most authentic source. Take the 1st volume of the census of 1901, which according to the minister himself is as much ahead of any other census that has ever been compiled as the Bible is ahead of the Toronto ' Globe.' I presume no pains are spared there to point out the imperfections ot the former census and the perfection of the last one.

Provision has been made for the first' time in a Dominion census for collecting figures of farm values

This will be information to the public.

and it can be premised that the data obtained will present a striking confirmation of the greatness of our agricultural industry, and of the leading place it occupies in the development of national life.
That is what I claim for the agricultural interests of this country. We are told by Mr. Blue that agriculture represents an investment of 72 per cent of the entire investment of capital iu the Dominion of Canada. We find that out of a total population of 'Canada of 5,'371,315, the urban population was 2,021,397, while the rural population was 3,349,516. I took occasion nearly a year ago to point out to the Minister of Agriculture the importance of not having his time distracted from agricultural concerns by the multiple, and in some cases useless things dumped into his department; and perhaps I cannot do better than quote the hon. gentleman's own language which I find on the Hansard of last year, page 3736. We were discussing the manner in which the agricultural affairs of Canada were conducted by the Imperial Institute in Britain, and the minister said :
The Board of Trade in England is one of the departments of government that is something like the Department of Agriculture here.
That is his own comparison.
It has a large number of branches connected generally with trade and commerce, and I think it is a department where they put a lot of different things that they do not quite know what to do with.
It is something like the Department of Agriculture in this country. Patents, trade marks and various things have been put into the Department of Agriculture here, although they have nothing whatever to do with agriculture. The Board of Trade seems to be an omnibus department.
What I do say, and I hope I will have the serious consideration of the hon. Minister of Agriculture, is that it is time that we had a department devoted purely, to agricultural concerns, having regard to the enormous interests that are involved, and if it is said that the hon. Minister of Agriculture will not have enough to do if he devotes his attention solely to agriculture, I may say that he can well spend a portion of his time in listening to the farmers of this country discussing the various practical questions that arise, and that they will give enormous interests uiat are involved ; and him a large amount of practical and valuable information. Mr. Clancy, then in the House, said :
He tells us that it is under the Board of Trade, which is an omnibus department, a sort of receptacle for worthless articles-things which are not good enough to keep, hut which it is hard to throw away.
And the minister apparently concurred in that view. Then the member for South Sim-coe calls the hon. minister's attention to it in another way. He says :
I wish to speak to the Minister of Agriculture as a farmer talking to a farmer. I presume the bon. gentleman is a practical farmer, and to that extent there is a bond of sympathy between us.
Then, skipping a few lines :
I think it was the president of the Board of Trade with whom we had all the difficulty in regard to the embargo on Canadian cattle ; and therefore I think the Minister of Agriculture should have approached this proposition with a good deal of suspicion on behalf of the farmers of Canada.
That seems to be emphasized to-day, having regard to the position of matters, when we find an ex-Minister of Agriculture in the old country urging what is not exactly fair in the interest of the farming community of this country. Then it is pointed out that this department is like a department in England-
No.

I may not probably be ih the judgment of one, but one swallow does

not make a summer-I will, at all events, be in the judgment of the great tribunal to which I turn with very much more regard than to hon. gentlemen on the other side, I shall be in the judgment of the people of Canada when I demand on behalf of the agriculturists of this country that a new order of things shall be inaugurated, and that instead of distracting the attention of the minister from the great duties which should be his and which, I am sure, he is anxious to discharge,, he shall concentrate his attention solely upon agricultural questions.

May I say a word as representing an agricultural constituency ? I do not think I need bring to the attention of the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) the condition in which agriculture, or the production of horses and cattle, is in my county, because I think he is perfectly well aware of it. If this information is to be collected in the same way the last census was taken, I must say, as representing that county, that I think we would be much better without it. The returns for agriculture have only been given some four years after the census is taken. If they were correct they were too late, but, as they were not correct, I can only hope that the people will look on them as ancient history, and that they will not judge our county according to the census as given. We have what we consider amongst the best farmers in the Dominion of Canada in our county, and we believe that our cattle are amongst the best, but the return given here would indicate that we are much behind our neighbours. I would like to read an article which shows that I am not speaking simply because I am in the House. I shall read this article from our local paper, a journal which, some years ago, members of the government appreciated very highly, although they may not appreciate it so highly now. I refer to the Huntingdon 1 Gleaner,' and the article that I would like to read is in regard to the last census. The date of his paper is 5th January, 1905. It says :
The census was taken in the spring of 1901 and we have only now the final volume, which relates to agriculture. Examination of the figures, we regret to say, shows they are not merely ancient history, but unreliable. The figures for dairy factories establish this. For instance we are assured there are no creameries in the county of Beauharnois (!), that there are twelve in Chateauguay, and eight in Huntingdon, and that Chateauguay sold nearly double the quantity of creamery butter that Huntingdon did. This is absurdly misleading. The figures for cheese are more approximately correct. The census declares six factories in Beauharnois made 364,000 lbs. of cheese, 14 in Chateauguay 1,112,000 lbs., and 19 in Huntingdon, 1,464,000 lbs. That the information here conveyed is erroneous can he shown in another way. The report declares there are 13,691 milch cows in Chateauguay and 18,489 in Huntingdon, yet the quantity of butter and cheese made by the two counties is about equal, the figures being : Mr. LENNOX.
Chateauguay 2,053,000 lbs., Huntingdon 2,084,000. Either the extra 4,798 cows with which Huntingdon is credited over Chateauguay must he what the Hon. Mr. Fisher terms ' robber cows,' or this census is not worth the paper it is printed od.
If that is a sample of the census we are going to get, I, on behalf of the agriculturists in the county of Huntingdon, object to this money being spent.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the section be adopted ?
We want an explanation of that Huntingdon business.

I am not in the position off-hand to explain a matter of that kind.
I can only say that a while ago my attention was drawn to another statement in the Huntingdon ' Gleaner ' which I did investigate, and which I found to be inaccurate according to the census returns and according to the facts. This statement- I have not seen before, but P will investigate it and report.

I would imagine that according to the practical agreement we came to, the minister had better move that the committee rise.
Mr. FISHER, I hope that facility will be given to the consideration of the Bill clause by clause when we next go into committee.
Progress reported.

maintopic: PACKING AND SALE OF CERTAIN COMMODITIES

speechtext:
Hon. SYDNEY FISHER (Minister of Agriculture) moved that the House go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, That it is expedient to amend the Act respecting the packing and sale of certain staple commodities, by inserting the following sections after section 4 :-
4a. When apples are packed in Canada for export for sale by the box they shall be packed in good and strong boxes of seasoned wood, the inside dimensions of which shall not be less than ten inches in depth, eleven inches in width and twenty inches in length, representing as near as possible two thousand two hundred cubic inches.
2. Every person who offers or exposes for sale, or vrho packs for export, apples by the box otherwise than in accordance with the foregoing provisions of this section shall he liable, on summary conviction, to a penalty of twenty-five cents for each box of apples so offered or exposed for sale or packed.
4b. When apples are packed in boxes or barrels having trays or fillers wherein it is intended to have a separate compartment for each apple, then the provisions of sections 4 and 4a shall not apply.

maintopic: PACKING AND SALE OF CERTAIN COMMODITIES
speechtext: Would the hon. minister explain the purpose of these resolutions ?

maintopic: PACKING AND SALE OF CERTAIN COMMODITIES
speechtext:
I may say that the purpose is to introduce a Bill to define the size

of boxes for tlie packing of apples. We have under a clause of the Staple Commodities Act, Chap. 26, Edward VII, 1 An Act respecting the packing and sale of certain commodities,' provision for the size of barrels for apples. Of late years our export trade in apples has been turning towards the use of boxes instead of barrels. For some time there .was a considerable variety in the dimensions of the boxes used. A little over a year ago the fruit growers and exporters asked for a standard box. At that time resolutions were passed by the fruitgrowers' associations in the different provinces, adopting what is known as the British Columbia box, the size of which is given in this resolution and I think I am safe in saying that there was a practically unanimous expression of opinion that this size was the most convenient, the most suitable and the one that would meet the demands of all parts of the country most completely. The Bill simply provides for the adoption of this stanuard and it also provides that the standard shall not apply to boxes where what are called ' fillers ' or pasteboard partitions are included, because there is a trade in this country in very choice apples both for export and sale in Canada and these apples are put into boxes like egg boxes with pasteboard compartments all through. Such a box requires to be a little larger to contain the same amount of fruit as the other boxes and its dimensions would depend considerably upon the size of the fruit selected for packing in a certain box. Therfore these boxes are omitted from the provisions of the Act.

maintopic: PACKING AND SALE OF CERTAIN COMMODITIES
speechtext: I see that the hon. minister here deals only with boxes. Is it not a fact that some provinces have different sized apple barrels?

maintopic: PACKING AND SALE OF CERTAIN COMMODITIES
speechtext: Not to-day. The law fixes a standard size of apple barrels.

maintopic: PACKING AND SALE OF CERTAIN COMMODITIES
speechtext: I understood that one province to-day ships in a barrel of a different size from the other provinces

maintopic: PACKING AND SALE OF CERTAIN COMMODITIES
speechtext: Not since the passage of the Act of 1901, the Act we are now amending, chapter 26 of 1901, 'An Act respecting the Packing and Sale of certain standard commodities.' The size of apple barrels is determined by the provision of section 4 of that Act to which this amended clause is intended to be added. The dimensions of the minimum barrel represent as nearly as possible 96 quarts. That is the minimum size, they can use a large size if they choose.

maintopic: PACKING AND SALE OF CERTAIN COMMODITIES
speechtext: That is the point I am getting at; some do use larger barrels. There are two classes of barrels used; that is why I asked the question.

maintopic: PACKING AND SALE OF CERTAIN COMMODITIES
speechtext:
The amendment does not apply to barrels at all except that clause 4b, the last part of the resolution, says that [DOT]- 221
when apples are packed in boxes or barrels having trays or fillers, the provisions of this Act shall not apply.

maintopic: PACKING AND SALE OF CERTAIN COMMODITIES
speechtext: Would it not be better to have the barrels all of one size, to adopt a standard size for all Canada and make it compulsory?

maintopic: PACKING AND SALE OF CERTAIN COMMODITIES
speechtext: The minimum size is fixed, and if people choose to use a larger barrel they will suffer a loss. Shippers are trying to get to the standard barrel as rapidly as they can. When the Act was passed, in 1901, it was thought best to leave the possibility of using a larger barrel if they chose, because at that time differnt sizes of barrels were used. Boxes, however, are not used to any very great extent and it is thought that a standard box can very soon be adopted.

maintopic: PACKING AND SALE OF CERTAIN COMMODITIES
speechtext: Will the minister tell me to what extent boxes are being used for the exportation of apples to the old country?

maintopic: PACKING AND SALE OF CERTAIN COMMODITIES
speechtext: I could not give the number of barrels or the quantity of apples exported in boxes but I may say that it is increasing from year to year very considerably. I am only making a guess but I am quite sure that not 10 per cent are sent in boxes. I doubt if 5 per cent of all the apples sent last season went in boxes.

maintopic: PACKING AND SALE OF CERTAIN COMMODITIES
speechtext: Has the shipment of apples in boxes been satisfactory ? Have the apples been largely bruised ?

maintopic: PACKING AND SALE OF CERTAIN COMMODITIES
speechtext: I think the trade in boxes has been very satisfactory. Apples shipped in boxes have as a rule returned better results than those shipped in barrels.

maintopic: PACKING AND SALE OF CERTAIN COMMODITIES
speechtext:
I understand that a few years ago in the United States, where the experience has been far greater than with us, a commission went thoroughly into the matter of box shipping versus barrel shipping, and reached the conclusion that the use of boxes was not satisfactory to the apple trade, and highly recommended barrels.
Mr. FISHER, That has not been the observation of our own fruit shippers at all, and in that respect I think we have not a great deal to learn from the United States.

maintopic: PACKING AND SALE OF CERTAIN COMMODITIES
speechtext:
What particular call is there, then, from the people of Canada for the box to replace the barrel ?
Mr. FISHER, ft is not proposed to require the box to replace the barrel. Nobody is trying to force anybody to substitute the box for the barrel. We are simply providing a standard box for those who choose to ship in boxes.

maintopic: PACKING AND SALE OF CERTAIN COMMODITIES
speechtext: Will the hon. minister tell us which is the cheaper, the barrel or the box ? During last year it is a fact that barrels were very scarce.

maintopic: PACKING AND SALE OF CERTAIN COMMODITIES
speechtext: I have no information on that point. The box as indicated in these dimensions has only one-third of the capacity of the standard barrel.

maintopic: PACKING AND SALE OF CERTAIN COMMODITIES
speechtext: The hon. minister tells us that he is providing for a standard box. I do not so understand the resolution, because it does not provide for a box of a uniform size. If we are going to have a standard box, one which may be used for measurement, we ought to make it uniform. Tt would be more convenient for packing in railway cars and in steam vessels than boxes of all sizes. We have provided for a ,strawberry box of uniform size, and if apples are to be sold by the box, I would strongly advise the minister to require that all the boxes shall be of the same size, so that the matter will be clearly understood both by the buyer and the seller.

maintopic: PACKING AND SALE OF CERTAIN COMMODITIES
speechtext: We are following in this proposed amendment the principle adopted in the law already in force in regard to the barrel, that is, that it shall not be less in size than a certain dimension.

maintopic: PACKING AND SALE OF CERTAIN COMMODITIES
speechtext: In both cases I think there is this defect, that if you want to compare prices per barrel, the barrels ought to be all of the same size, and for the same reason the boxes ought to be all of the same size. Then people will know wliat the market is.

maintopic: PACKING AND SALE OF CERTAIN COMMODITIES
speechtext: As a matter of fact, it is found that the shippers try to get the smallest barrel that will pass, and the same would probably be the case with regard to the box. If we provide positively that the box shall be of such and such measurement and no other, a person using a box a little larger than that measurement might be punished for an infraction of the law ; but if a person sees that the box is not smaller than the permissible size, he may use one a little larger if he chooses. It is thought that there should be that degree of elasticity and freedom in regard to the size of the box or barrel. 1 may say that the resolution of the Fruit Growers' Association asked that a minimum size of box should be made law.

maintopic: PACKING AND SALE OF CERTAIN COMMODITIES
speechtext: The hon. minister has mentioned one fruit growers' association. There is more than one fruit growers' association in Canada, and unless a Bill of this nature is asked for by a large majority of the fruit growers' associations,. I would hesitate before giving it my support. One objection I have to it at first sight is that the size of the box is not uniform. However, I would rather trust the opinion of the fruit growers' associations in different parts of the country on this point, and if the minister could give us any information as to the number of associations he has corresponded with, and as to their opinions with regard to this measure, that would go some distance in enabling us to come to a conclusion with regard to it.

maintopic: PACKING AND SALE OF CERTAIN COMMODITIES
PACKING AND SALE OF CERTAIN COMMODITIES
speechtext: I am informed that these dimensions are the dimensions of the standard British Columbia box, which has been adopted after full discussion by the fruit growers' of that province, that the question was discussed by the Ontario Fruit Growers' Association, who passed a resolution endorsing and adopting that box, that that was followed by a resolution of the Nova Scotia Fruit Growers' Association and the Prince Edward Island Fruit Growers' Association, and that the details were worked out by the officers of my department at the request of the firuit growers' associations who desired to get a uniform standard.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: PACKING AND SALE OF CERTAIN COMMODITIES
speechtext: I think the details of this measure had better be discussed in committee.

maintopic: PACKING AND SALE OF CERTAIN COMMODITIES
speechtext:
I may say that I heartily appreciate the provision made in this Bill for a uniform box for the export of apples ; and in answer to my hon. friend from Halton (Mr. Henderson) I may say that there will not be any difficulty about getting the shippers to use boxes of practically uniform size. When apples are sold by the box in Great Britain, each box will naturally be expected to contain about the same, quantity, and it will be in the interest of the shippers to use a box that will approach as nearly as possible to the size provided for in this Bill. Regarding tin; size that is suggested, my opinion, from experience in the handling of apples in boxes to a considerable extent, is that a better size would be a trifle shorter and a trifle wider, namely, twelve and a half inches wide by eighteen inches long rather than eleven by twenty. That would give practically the same space and contain the same quantity, and as near as possible represent a bushel. The boxes made in Unit way would be a little bit stronger with the same weight of lumber. In our experience of shipping in boxes, the desire is to get the lumber as light and also as strong as possible. I am not saying this so much in a spirit of criticism as for the purpose of giving my opinion after an experience in shipping many thousands of boxes, which I have done because I was unable to get sufficient barrels. We found that this size made a stronger and a better looking box and one in every respect more suitable than the size indicated in the Bill. Of course I know that the Fruit Grower's Association have suggested this size, which is largely owing to the fact of their having used this size, especially in the Niagara District. The firm which made this size of boxes sold them almost entirely in that district, and the shorter and wider box was not used there to any considerable extent, if at all. I merely throw this out as a suggestion, in case the hon. minister is not perfectly convinced that the size stated in the Bill is the right size. I think we should endeav-

our to have the best possible box because boxes are going to be used in the future much more than they were iu the past. The difficulty in getting barrels and their increased cost is becoming a very important factor in the export trade of apples, and I believe that the day is coming when the boxes will be much more largely used. As yet the trade in England, especially in Liverpool, seems to prefer the barrel, but on the other hand, Glasgow and Hamburg seem to be much more ready to accept the box ; and I may say that this last season we got decidedly the best returns from the boxes we exported to Glasgow. I think it would be advisable to have the dimensions varied a trifle because then the box will be stronger. It is hardly necessary that 1 should enter into an explanation why it is stronger except that the shorter box does not bulge at the sides or the bottom and top so readily. I must congratulate the minister on the outworking of the Fruit Marks Act. With regard to the minimum size of the barrel and the working out of the Act touching the handling and packing of the fruit and its quality, it was a step in the right direction.
Motion agreed to, and House went into Committee on the resolution.

maintopic: PACKING AND SALE OF CERTAIN COMMODITIES
speechtext: Is it the intention to -make this provision regarding the boxes * apply to fruit for sale in this country as well as for export ? The section reads ' Expose for sale or for export.'

maintopic: PACKING AND SALE OF CERTAIN COMMODITIES
speechtext: The clause as printed here in the resolution was intended to cover the same point as section 4 with regard to barrels. In section 4 the wording is a little different, and my hon. colleague the Minister of Justice says he would interpret it to mean only when packed for export, but subsection is worded just the same as the resolution and what would apply to sales in Canada as well as for export.

maintopic: PACKING AND SALE OF CERTAIN COMMODITIES
speechtext: The minister does not intend to do that.

maintopic: PACKING AND SALE OF CERTAIN COMMODITIES
speechtext: I am not quite prepared to say. The resolutions, as passed by the Fruit Grower's Association were intended to apply to the sale in Canada as well as to the sales for export.

maintopic: PACKING AND SALE OF CERTAIN COMMODITIES
speechtext: That would be unjust.

maintopic: PACKING AND SALE OF CERTAIN COMMODITIES
speechtext: But I may say that the Act at present, so far as barrels are concerned, does not apply to sales in the country, but only for export. Under these circumstances, I think I must consider the matter asking the House to concur in that resolution.

maintopic: PACKING AND SALE OF CERTAIN COMMODITIES
speechtext:
I should think the minister might say at once that he would amend it so that it would not be open to that construction. Surely the minister is not going to incorporate in the law a provision
which will prevent a farmer from taking apples in a box of any size or capacity up from his farm and selling them wherever he likes. What the minister means to say, I take it, is : Every person who offers for export, or who exposes for sale for export, or who packs for export, apples by the box otherwise than in accordance with the foregoing provisions.

maintopic: PACKING AND SALE OF CERTAIN COMMODITIES
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: PACKING AND SALE OF CERTAIN COMMODITIES
speechtext:
I would like to say a word with reference to the packing in boxes and the shape of the boxes. As a retailer of thirty-two years experience, I think I ought to know something about the selling of apples. When you sell apples by the barrel you have a great deal more difficulty than when you sell them by the box, for two reasons :	Every consumer is not able to
buy a barrel, but there are few who would not buy a half barrel or box. Another thing is that when a man buys a barrel of apples and puts it in his cellar, if it is warm there, the result probably is that before the barrel is half used the apples spoil with the heat, or shrink and become practically valueless. If the apples are packed in a box, you have a better package to sell and to expose for sale. A's to the shape of the box, I think that the nearer you get to a cube the better. For example, everybody must have noticed and every retail dealer knows-that formerly we bought most of our oranges from Mediterranean countries. They were packed in boxes, but the boxes were of miserable quality and not of good size. But when oranges began to come from California, we found them to reach this market in boxes of fine quality and uniform size, and nearly square so that they presented a good appearance when the cover was taken off and the fruit exposed in the window or on the shelf. The trade in oranges and lemons from Mediterranean countries has become almost extinct in this market. If any one will notice as he walks along Sparks Street or Bank Street and passes the windows of the retail grocers, he will see that nearly every one of the boxes containing oranges bears the name of Stewart, a packer in California who has made a world-wide reputation in the sale of oranges. If the box is longer than it is broad, there is a partition which divides it into two compartments each nearly cubical in form. If you take a box of prunes that comes from Oregon or California you will see that the same method is followed. The boxes are good, the packing neat and nice, and every box, when the cover is taken off and the fruit exposed in the window or on the shelf, makes a good appearance. If you can get apples packed in boxes, the nearer you can approach this size and style of box the better for the retail trade, and I believe, for the packer and the grower also. And if you fix a minimum size, I do not think there is any danger of the packer making a larger box-he is not given to that kind of

thing. X would like to have it understood that a uniform size should be established and, if that is done, the box should be nearer square than oblong.

maintopic: PACKING AND SALE OF CERTAIN COMMODITIES
speechtext: My hon. friend opposite (Mr. Sproule) has drawn my attention to the wording of this clause and I feel that that wording must be changed. But I would not venture, at the moment to propose the exact change to be made, therefore I think it would be better to ask the committee to rise and report progress and ask leave to sit again so that at a future sitting, I can bring in the wording properly drawn up.

maintopic: PACKING AND SALE OF CERTAIN COMMODITIES
speechtext: Before the motion is put, I would like to ask the minister when he will be likely to move the House again into committee on this resolution. Shall we have time to communicate with our constituents before that is done ?

maintopic: PACKING AND SALE OF CERTAIN COMMODITIES
speechtext:
Yes, I will not ask for committee again for a few days.
Progress reported.
Sir WILLIAM MULOCIi moved the adjournment of the House.
Will the hon. minister (Sir William Mulock) say what business we shall take up to-morrow ?
To morrow is a private members' day.
But, if we get through with private members' business ?

If we get through with that, we shall probably go into supply, and, in that case, take up the estimates of the Minister of Public Works. There will be no objection, I suppose, to making some progress ?
On the same principle as the last day !
Motion agreed to, and the House adjourned at 9.50 p.m.
Wednesday, February 8, 1905.
